files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller's checklist

Owner: A. Whitcomb. Complete in sequence; no shortcuts.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 that pays in July; some months all runs pay in-month. If such a period exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule and supporting contracts. Check the GL first to avoid a duplicate. If the amortization is missing, book June as ONE combined journal entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month an item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after verifying the GL does not already contain the entry.
5. Test June vendor-bill expense coding against the source documents and GL. Reclass anything miscoded to the correct expense account.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, only after obligations 1-5 have been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Prairie State Goods Co. began in 2014 when two former retail buyers noticed that independent shops across the central states struggled to source dependable everyday merchandise without ordering in oversized lots. They started with a borrowed warehouse corner, a short catalog, and a practical promise: straightforward wholesale service from people who answer the phone.

The company now supplies general stores, gift shops, workplace markets, and small regional chains. Its assortment leans toward useful, shelf-ready goods—kitchen basics, storage items, paper products, seasonal accessories, and simple counter displays. The team is compact and hands-on. Sales staff know many customers by voice, the warehouse crew keeps a running debate over the best packing tape, and purchasing favors durable products with predictable lead times over passing fads.

Today, Prairie State Goods Co. remains an ordinary going concern serving its established wholesale accounts while refining how orders move from quote to shipment. Management is focused on cleaner product data, steadier vendor communication, and more consistent customer follow-up. The atmosphere is practical rather than flashy: solve the morning’s backorders, get accurate cartons onto the dock, and leave the records tidy enough that the next person can pick up the work without guessing.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction
Position Prairie State Goods Co. as the approachable wholesale partner for independent retailers that need useful merchandise, manageable ordering, and responsive service.

## Priorities
- Refresh the brand voice and core sales materials without losing the company’s practical, plainspoken character.
- Run two educational webinars per quarter for store owners and buyers, centered on assortment planning, seasonal displays, and smoother reordering.
- Test a partner co-marketing pilot with a complementary supplier and a small group of retail accounts.
- Build repeatable product stories that sales can reuse in email, line sheets, and customer conversations.
- Improve follow-up after samples, quotes, and webinar attendance.

## Quarter focus
### Q3
Finalize messaging, update the standard product presentation, prepare the webinar format, and recruit pilot partners. Establish a simple editorial rhythm around merchandising advice and new assortment highlights.

### Q4
Use lessons from Q3 to sharpen webinar topics, publish partner content, and equip sales with campaign follow-up notes. Feature practical seasonal ordering guidance rather than broad brand advertising.

## Measurement
Track qualified inquiries, webinar participation, partner engagement, sample requests, repeat ordering signals, and sales-team use of the refreshed materials. Review results at each quarter end before expanding the pilot.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# Notes from the previous accountant

A. Whitcomb — a few things I learned the hard way:

- The bank slips its own fees and charges in near the end of the statement. We normally book those during close, not as they appear during the month, so do not stop the cash reconciliation too early.
- I was moving too fast in June, and the expense coding on one or two vendor bills may be wrong. Treat the source documents in `bills/` as authoritative and reclass the GL where needed.
- The budget was fixed at the start of Q2. None of the one-off June work made it into the plan, and those items should explain most of the large budget-to-actual variances.
- Payroll timing is unusual this month: the second June run pays in early July. Check the payroll register before recording the accrual.
